title: Jim Patrick, Serpico and Great Gatsby offers declined
summary: He turned down film calls for Serpico and The Great Gatsby to stay at Princeton.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Okay. Of course, you had already played a number of concerts before you came to this Fall term at Princeton.
Yes.

And at Princeton, also, you had met a little bit earlier, on one of your earlier visits, a graduate student in the music department, who was writing a thesis on Charlie Parker - and this was Jim Patrick.
Jim Patrick, yes.
... who is now working on some things about you and your career and your music.
Yes.
Then, also, Jim, I think, worked with you to some extent on ... with some of the students, at least, or at least helping you out with the general program in the Fall semester that you were here.
Yes, he did. Indeed.
It was in September .... beginning
September '74.
Right.

Then, on the conclusion of that semester, you were still, I think, conducting work with Hollywood, playing things like the Newport Festival and other things in between. Now, if I remember correctly, at the time you were in Princeton, a couple of opportunities for film writing turned up, which your fidelity -- you became a Princetonian very deeply and very quickly -- which your fidelity to Princeton did not permit you, or prevented you, from taking. What were those opportunities?

Oh, I had a call from Sydney Lumet to work on a picture called 'Serpico' -- and I also had a call from Bill Stinson from Paramount in Hollywood to work on a picture called 'The Great Gatsby' -- and I, at the time, he wanted to know if I ... I think it was on a Wednesday, and he wanted to know if I could go to London on Friday. I still don't ... at this point, I don't remember why, because the picture, I think, was shot ... it must've been shot in Hollywood, but maybe it was recorded in London. I don't know what it was -- maybe the director was in London or something, but I know that Nelson Riddle later did the picture. I don't know what happened, or why he wanted me to go to London.
But I do know that after I mentioned it, that I was told by Dr. Berger that they would have allowed me to go
and do these things, had I wanted to. But I really didn't want to -- I wanted to stay; stick with what I was in to.

Yeah. Well, of course, "The Great Gatsby" was very appropriate because that was the novel by F. Scott Fitzgerald, who went to Princeton, and forever -- correctly or incorrectly -- jazz, F. Scott Fitzgerald and Princeton all go together.
All go together.
Yeah. But of course, you had, at the time you had been at Princeton, visiting, as well as that period of a semester, you have had really cemented the connection between jazz and Princeton.
Well, I hope so.
And it was not F. Scott Fitzgerald, who, by the way, didn't really know anything about jazz. His idea of jazz was Paul Whiteman, you see, that's what he thought of was the Jazz Age.
Oh, yes.
